# Investigative Report: Linking the Ronin Bridge and Harmony Horizon Bridge Thefts to Lazarus Group

## Executive assessment

The available public evidence supports a strong link between the March 2022 Ronin Bridge theft and the June 2022 Harmony Horizon Bridge theft through three overlapping elements: **public attribution to North Korea’s Lazarus Group, similar laundering behaviors, and blockchain-wallet activity consistent with a coordinated North Korean hacking operation**.

The Ronin theft involved approximately **173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC**, valued at approximately **$540 million when the theft occurred**. The Harmony Horizon Bridge theft involved approximately **$99.7 million**, commonly described as a $100 million theft. Elliptic attributed the Ronin theft to Lazarus Group in March 2022, with the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) subsequently identifying the relevant Ethereum address as belonging to Lazarus Group. In May 2023, the FBI publicly confirmed that Lazarus Group was responsible for the Harmony theft. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The laundering evidence is also materially consistent. In both cases, the stolen assets were moved through intermediary wallets, decentralized exchanges, cross-chain mechanisms, and privacy-enhancing services. The Ronin laundering pattern included conversion of USDC into ETH, use of Tornado Cash, swaps into Bitcoin, Bitcoin mixing, and eventual movement toward crypto-to-fiat services. The Harmony laundering pattern included programmatic structuring through Tornado Cash, later movement through Railgun, and deposits into centralized exchanges including Binance and Huobi. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/); [Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

In my assessment, the evidence is sufficient to conclude that the two thefts are linked at the **public attribution and behavioral-pattern levels**. The provided materials do not, however, contain specific wallet addresses, transaction hashes, or a direct wallet-to-wallet bridge between the Ronin and Harmony cases. They therefore support a high-confidence **group-level linkage**, but not an independently reproducible address-level proof based solely on the supplied material. The supplied sources also do not establish that Lazarus Group is identical to **APT38**. That relationship should remain unconfirmed in this report.

## Scope and source assessment

This report uses only the four source URLs supplied in the case materials. The materials contain three substantive case reports and one Elliptic resource-index page.

| Source ID | Publisher and date | Primary evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Elliptic, March 29, 2022 | Initial attribution and laundering analysis for the Ronin theft; later OFAC attribution |
| S2 | Chainalysis, September 8, 2022 | Laundering typology, cross-chain tracing, and seizure information for Ronin funds |
| S3 | Elliptic, May 9, 2023 | FBI confirmation of Lazarus attribution for Harmony; Tornado Cash and Railgun tracing |
| S4 | Elliptic resource page | General Elliptic research index; no additional substantive case evidence in the supplied content |

The strongest evidence is S3 for Harmony because it reports an FBI confirmation, and S1 for Ronin because it records the subsequent OFAC designation of the relevant Ethereum address. S2 provides useful corroboration from an independent blockchain-analytics company concerning Ronin’s laundering stages and the seizure of more than $30 million. S4 is not relied upon for any material factual conclusion because the supplied text is an index page rather than a case-specific report.

## Case 1: Ronin Bridge theft

### Attack and value

The Ronin Network theft was announced on March 29, 2022, after occurring six days earlier. The stolen assets consisted of **173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC**. Elliptic valued the theft at approximately **$540 million at the time of the theft**, while noting that the assets were worth more than **$615 million when the exploit was discovered**, reflecting cryptocurrency price changes. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

According to the cited postmortem summary, the attacker obtained the private keys of **five of Ronin’s nine validator nodes**, which was sufficient to authorize withdrawals. The attack was assessed by Ronin as socially engineered rather than the result of a technical flaw in the bridge’s smart-contract logic. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

### Attribution

Elliptic reported that OFAC identified the Ethereum address associated with the theft as belonging to **Lazarus Group**, described in the source as a North Korean state hacking group. The OFAC action prohibited U.S. persons and entities from transacting with that address. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

This is significant because the attribution was not limited to a private analytical assessment by Elliptic. The source reports a subsequent public sanctions action by a U.S. government authority identifying the address as Lazarus Group-linked. On the evidence provided, the Ronin attribution is therefore supported by both private-sector analysis and government action.

### Laundering pattern

The Ronin laundering sequence described by Chainalysis contains approximately five stages:

1. Stolen Ether was sent to intermediary wallets.
2. Ether was mixed in batches using Tornado Cash.
3. Ether was exchanged for Bitcoin.
4. Bitcoin was mixed in batches.
5. Bitcoin was deposited with crypto-to-fiat services for cash-out.

Chainalysis also reported that more than **12,000 cryptocurrency addresses** had been used in the laundering process at the time of publication. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

Elliptic described an initial phase in which the stolen USDC was exchanged for ETH through decentralized exchanges. This reduced exposure to asset issuers that might freeze stablecoins and avoided the screening associated with centralized exchanges. The attacker then moved approximately **$16.7 million in ETH through three centralized exchanges**, before shifting toward Tornado Cash after the exchanges publicly indicated that they would cooperate with law enforcement. Elliptic reported that approximately **$80.3 million in ETH** had been sent through Tornado Cash by April 14, 2022, with another **$9.7 million** held in intermediary wallets apparently prepared for laundering. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

The exact figures reported by Elliptic and Chainalysis are not necessarily intended to be identical. They were published on different dates, used different analytical methodologies, and may refer to different stages or categories of the movement. The common pattern, however, is clear: rapid movement through intermediary wallets, asset conversion, use of mixers, and attempts to reach cash-out points.

## Case 2: Harmony Horizon Bridge theft

### Attack and value

The Harmony Horizon Bridge was exploited on June 24, 2022, for approximately **$99.7 million**, generally rounded to $100 million. Elliptic described the bridge as servicing the Harmony blockchain and noted prior concerns that it was overly centralized and therefore vulnerable to social engineering. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The supplied evidence does not provide the individual wallet addresses involved in the Harmony theft. It does, however, describe the movement of the stolen funds through specific privacy-oriented services and exchanges.

### Attribution

Elliptic reported that the **FBI confirmed Lazarus Group’s responsibility** for the Harmony Horizon Bridge theft. The FBI confirmation also validated Elliptic’s earlier assessment, which had been based on similarities between the Harmony laundering activity and patterns observed in prior Lazarus-linked blockchain thefts. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

This is the strongest direct link between Harmony and the Lazarus-linked Ronin case: the Harmony report explicitly states that the attribution was based in part on similarities with the laundering methods used after the Ronin Bridge theft. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

### Laundering pattern

After the Harmony theft, the attackers programmatically structured transactions through **Tornado Cash**, an Ethereum-based decentralized mixer. Elliptic stated that the laundering methods mirrored those used to conceal funds from the Ronin Bridge theft. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

Elliptic estimated that more than **$555 million** from the Ronin and Harmony thefts had been sent through Tornado Cash: more than **$468 million from Ronin** and approximately **$96 million from Harmony**. The source characterized this combined activity as approximately **5.8% of nearly $9 billion** in total funds sent through Tornado Cash at that time. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

After Tornado Cash sanctions, the Harmony funds were later moved through **Railgun**, a privacy-oriented decentralized-finance protocol. Elliptic estimated that approximately **70% of the Ether passing through Railgun** at the relevant time represented funds from the Harmony theft. The report argued that this unusually high concentration made the mixing less effective because the anonymity set was comparatively small. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The funds were subsequently deposited into three crypto-asset exchanges. Elliptic reported that Binance and Huobi identified, blocked, and seized a portion of the funds. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

## Comparative linkage analysis

| Linkage dimension | Ronin Bridge | Harmony Horizon Bridge | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public attribution | OFAC identified the relevant Ethereum address as Lazarus Group | FBI confirmed Lazarus Group responsibility | Strong group-level linkage |
| Attack context | Cross-chain bridge theft involving validator-key compromise | Cross-chain bridge theft; source describes centralization and social-engineering exposure | Similar target type and attack context, but not proof by itself |
| Initial laundering | Intermediary wallets, DEX conversion, ETH movement | Programmatic structuring through Tornado Cash | Consistent use of staged laundering |
| Privacy services | Tornado Cash; later cross-chain DeFi activity | Tornado Cash followed by Railgun | Strong behavioral overlap |
| Cross-chain behavior | Chain-hopping across Ethereum, BNB Chain, and BitTorrent Chain | Movement through Ethereum-based privacy infrastructure and exchanges | Consistent with multi-chain concealment |
| Exchange exposure | More than $30 million seized with industry and law-enforcement cooperation | Binance and Huobi blocked and seized part of the funds | Similar cash-out disruption pattern |
| Address-level evidence in supplied material | No readable addresses supplied | No readable addresses supplied | Direct wallet linkage cannot be independently reconstructed |

The clearest linkage is not simply that both were bridge attacks. It is that the same actor attribution is supported by government statements and that the laundering behavior displays repeated operational characteristics: intermediary wallets, automated or structured transfers, asset swaps, mixers, cross-chain movement, and attempts to reach centralized exchanges or cash-out points.

Chainalysis specifically described North Korea’s “typical DeFi laundering technique” as a sequence involving intermediary wallets, Tornado Cash, conversion to Bitcoin, Bitcoin mixing, and crypto-to-fiat services. It also reported that, after OFAC sanctions against Tornado Cash, the Ronin-linked actors used DeFi services to chain-hop across multiple assets and blockchains. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

## Wallet evidence and limitations

The supplied evidence refers to wallet activity but does not reproduce wallet addresses or transaction hashes. The Ronin evidence identifies a thief’s Ethereum address through the OFAC attribution described by Elliptic, while the Harmony evidence describes clusters of intermediary addresses, post-Tornado withdrawals, Railgun deposits, and exchange deposits. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

Accordingly, the wallet evidence supports the following limited conclusions:

- Wallet activity was central to attribution and laundering analysis.
- The Ronin activity included thousands of addresses and multiple laundering stages.
- The Harmony activity included intermediary wallets, Tornado Cash, Railgun, and exchange deposits.
- The two cases shared laundering infrastructure and transaction-structuring characteristics.
- The supplied materials do not permit an independent analyst to reproduce the complete transaction graph or identify a specific wallet that directly transferred funds from the Ronin cluster to the Harmony cluster.

This limitation matters. A behavioral similarity is probative, but it is not equivalent to a cryptographic or transaction-level proof. The public attribution evidence substantially strengthens the linkage, particularly because the FBI confirmation for Harmony and OFAC attribution for Ronin independently point to Lazarus Group. Nevertheless, the report should not claim a direct wallet bridge that is not shown in the provided materials.

## Lazarus Group and APT38

The task refers to “Lazarus Group/APT38.” The supplied sources identify Lazarus Group and describe it as North Korean-backed or state-linked, but they do **not** mention the designation “APT38.” No source provided here establishes that the Ronin and Harmony operations were conducted by an entity specifically labeled APT38, nor does any supplied source explain whether APT38 is a synonym, subordinate unit, or separate designation from Lazarus Group.

Therefore, the defensible conclusion is:

> The Ronin and Harmony thefts are publicly linked to Lazarus Group. The supplied evidence does not independently establish an APT38 attribution or a Lazarus Group–APT38 equivalence.

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a strong and concrete conclusion that the Ronin Bridge and Harmony Horizon Bridge thefts are linked through Lazarus Group attribution and repeated laundering behavior. Ronin was publicly associated with Lazarus Group through OFAC attribution of the relevant Ethereum address, while the FBI later confirmed Lazarus Group responsibility for Harmony. The laundering patterns in both cases involved intermediary wallets, structured transaction flows, asset conversion, Tornado Cash, cross-chain or DeFi-based obfuscation, and attempted movement into centralized exchanges.

The relationship is strongest at the level of **actor attribution and operational methodology**. It is weaker at the level of directly demonstrable wallet-to-wallet continuity because the supplied materials do not include the relevant addresses or transaction identifiers. The sources support a high-confidence assessment that the same North Korea-linked hacking organization, publicly identified as Lazarus Group, conducted both thefts or controlled the laundering operations associated with both incidents. They do not support a separate, source-grounded conclusion that the actor should specifically be labeled APT38.

Cryptocurrency Community Is Making It Difficult for North Korean Hackers To Profit September 8, 2022 | Erin Plante One of the most troubling trends in crypto crime right now is the stunning rise in funds stolen from DeFi protocols , and in particular cross-chain bridges . Much of the value stolen from DeFi protocols can be attributed to bad actors affiliated with North Korea, especially elite hacking units like Lazarus Group. We estimate that so far in 2022, North Korea-linked groups have stolen approximately $1 billion of cryptocurrency from DeFi protocols. But today I had the privilege of joining the Axie Infinity team on stage at AxieCon to deliver some good news: With the help of law enforcement and leading organizations in the cryptocurrency industry, more than $30 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers has been seized. This marks the first time ever that cryptocurrency stolen by a North Korean hacking group has been seized, and we’re confident it won’t be the last. These are the results thus far of our investigation following the March 2022 theft of more than $600 million from Ronin Network, a sidechain built for the play-to-earn game Axie Infinity. I am proud to say that the Chainalysis Crypto Incident Response team played a role in these seizures, utilizing advanced tracing techniques to follow stolen funds to cash out points and liaising with law enforcement and industry players to quickly freeze funds. The seizures represent approximately 10% of the total funds stolen from Axie Infinity (accounting for price differences between time stolen and seized), and demonstrate that it is becoming more difficult for bad actors to successfully cash out their ill-gotten crypto gains. We have proven that with the right blockchain analysis tools, world-class investigators and compliance professionals can collaborate to stop even the most sophisticated hackers and launderers. There is still work to be done, but this is a milestone in our efforts to make the cryptocurrency ecosystem safer. So, how did we do it? Here’s what we can share now. How the Ronin Bridge was hacked & the stolen funds were laundered The attack began when the Lazarus Group gained access to five of the nine private keys held by transaction validators for Ronin Network’s cross-chain bridge. They used this majority to approve two transactions, both withdrawals: one for 173,600 ether (ETH) and the other for 25.5 million USD Coin (USDC). They then initiated their laundering process – and Chainalysis began tracing the funds. The laundering of these funds has leveraged over 12,000 different crypto addresses to-date, which demonstrates the hackers’ highly sophisticated laundering capabilities. North Korea’s typical DeFi laundering technique has roughly five stages: Stolen Ether sent to intermediary wallets Ether mixed in batches using Tornado Cash Ether swapped for bitcoin Bitcoin mixed in batches Bitcoin deposited to crypto-to-fiat services for cashout Lazarus Group has replicated this process with large portions of Ronin’s stolen funds. We can visualize it below using Chainalysis Reactor: However, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) recently sanctioned Tornado Cash for its role in laundering over $455 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Axie Infinity. Since then, Lazarus Group has moved away from the popular Ethereum mixer, instead leveraging DeFi services to chain hop, or switch between several different kinds of cryptocurrencies in a single transaction. Bridges serve an important function to move digital assets between chains and most usage of these platforms is completely legitimate. Lazarus appears to be using bridges in an attempt to obscure source of funds. With Chainalysis tools these cross chain funds movements are easily traced. We can use Chainalysis Storyline to see an example of how Lazarus Group utilized chain-hopping to launder some of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity: Above, we see that the hacker bridged ETH from the Ethereum blockchain to the BNB chain and then swapped that ETH for USDD, which was then bridged to the BitTorrent chain. Lazarus Group carried out hundreds of similar transactions across several blockchains to launder the funds they stole from Axie Infinity, in addition to the more conventional Tornado Cash-based laundering we covered above. Transparency and collaboration are key Cryptocurrency’s transparency is instrumental to investigating hacks like the one suffered by Axie Infinity. Investigators with the right tools can follow the money to understand and disrupt a cybercrime organization’s laundering activities. This would never be possible in traditional financial channels, where money laundering usually involves networks of shell companies and financial institutions in jurisdictions that may not cooperate. Even so, these seizures would not have been possible without collaboration across the public and private sectors. Much of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity remain unspent in cryptocurrency wallets under the hackers’ control. We look forward to continuing to work with the cryptocurrency ecosystem to prevent them and other illicit actors from cashing out their funds. The total value of the stolen cryptoassets at the time of the theft was $540 million. This is the second largest crypto theft of all time. On April 14th, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions against the thief's Ethereum address and listed the owner of this address as Lazarus Group – the North Korean state hacking group . The sanctions prohibit US persons and entities from transacting with this address to ensure the state-sponsored group can’t cash out any further funds they continue to hold onto through US-based crypto exchanges. The incident occurred six days before the exploit was announced by Ronin. Amid confusion over the delayed response, it announced that the exploit was only discovered after a 5,000 ETH withdrawal attempt from one of their users failed. At the time of discovery, the stolen funds were worth over $615 million. How the hack unfolded How the hack unfolded According to a postmortem published by Ronin, the theft came as a result of an attacker hacking the “validator nodes”of the Ronin bridge. Funds can be moved out if five of the nine validators approve it. The attacker managed to get hold of the private cryptographic keys belonging to five of the validators, which was enough to steal the cryptoassets. The post mortem claims that “all evidence points to this attack being socially engineered, rather than a technical flaw ”. Laundering the stolen crypto Laundering the stolen crypto Elliptic’s internal analysis indicates that the attacker has managed to launder 18% of their stolen funds as of April 14th. First, the stolen USDC was swapped for ETH through decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to prevent it from being seized. Tokens such as stablecoins are controlled by their issuers, who in some cases can freeze tokens involved in illicit activity. By converting the tokens at DEXs, the hacker avoided the anti-money laundering (AML) and 'know your customer' (KYC) checks performed at centralized exchanges. This is an increasingly common tactic seen in hacks of this type, as described in Elliptic’s recent report: “ DeFi: Risk, Regulation, and the Rise of DeCrime ” . However, the attacker then began laundering $16.7 million worth of ETH through three centralized exchanges. This strategy is uncommon for typical DeFi exploits given these exchanges’ AML obligations, though it has been observed more often in past Lazarus group-affiliated exploits. As the affected exchanges publicly announced that they would work with law enforcement to establish their identity, the attacker changed their laundering strategy to instead make use of Tornado Cash – a popular smart contract-based mixer on the Ethereum blockchain. Ongoing transactions have so far sent $80.3 million worth of ETH through Tornado Cash. Destination of $107 million ETH of the stolen $540 million ETH & USDC. The attacker’s blockchain activity shows that another $9.7 million worth of ETH is in intermediary wallets prepared to be laundered, most likely also through Tornado Cash. This leaves a considerable $433 million remaining in the attacker’s original wallet. Elliptic investigators are tracking these stolen funds, and have labelled the addresses associated to this attacker in our systems – ensuring that our clients will be alerted if they receive any of these funds. How the Lazarus Group is laundering its funds. Source: Elliptic Forensics . Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group refers to a group of North Korean state hackers who have been targeting crypto entities since at least 2017. Until 2021, the majority of this activity was directed towards centralized exchanges located in South Korea or elsewhere in Asia. However, within the past year the group’s attention has turned to DeFi services. While the service that was attacked in this instance – Ronin Network’s bridge – is decentralized, the creators of the network Sky Mavis are located in Vietnam. It is somewhat unsurprising that this attack has been attributed to North Korea. Many features of the attack mirrored the method used by Lazarus Group in previous high-profile attacks, including the location of the victim, the attack method (believed to have involved social engineering) and the laundering pattern utilized by the group after the event. Many commentators believe that cryptoassets stolen by Lazarus Group are used to fund the state’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs. With recent reports that North Korea may be again preparing for nuclear testing, today’s sanctions activity highlights the importance of ensuring that Lazarus Group is not able to successfully launder the proceeds of these attacks. The announcement confirms Elliptic’s previous attribution of the $100 million hack to North Korea, which we were the first to identify after numerous similarities were observed with Lazarus’ past blockchain laundering patterns. This is a preview of our upcoming briefing note into tracing the stolen funds from the Harmony Horizon Hack to North Korea, including the demixing of the funds through Tornado Cash and Railgun. Horizon – a cross-chain bridge servicing the Harmony blockchain – was exploited on June 24th 2022 for $99.7 million. Concerns had previously been raised that the bridge was over-centralized, meaning that it was particularly vulnerable to social engineering attacks – a common attack vector for the Lazarus Group. Similar issues resulted in the criminal organization stealing over $540 million from another cross-chain bridge called Ronin earlier in March 2022. After stealing the funds from Horizon, the Lazarus Group then programmatically structured transactions through Tornado Cash, which is a decentralized Ethereum-based mixer. Elliptic researchers identified that the laundering methods employed mirrored those the Lazarus Group had used when attempting to conceal funds from the Ronin Bridge hack, which had also been sent through Tornado Cash. US sanctions US sanctions Tornado Cash was subsequently sanctioned by the US Treasury in August 2022, with Secretary of State Anthony Blinken citing its prolific use by the Lazarus Group to launder funds from its past hacks. Elliptic’s research suggests that the Lazarus Group sent more than $555 million through Tornado Cash from these hacks, including more than $468 million from the Ronin hack and $96 million from the Harmony hack. This North Korea-linked activity accounts for approximately 5.8% of the nearly $9 billion in total funds sent through the Tornado Cash mixer to date. Elliptic has traced the stolen funds from the Horizon hack through Tornado Cash. Our forthcoming briefing note will break down the methodology we used and how it ultimately aided the eventual attribution of the exploit to the Lazarus Group. The post-Tornado withdrawals were initially placed into several addresses, where they remained dormant until January 2023. Elliptic has previously identified Railgun as a prime alternative to Tornado Cash following sanctions against the latter. You can read more about Railgun – and other Ethereum-based privacy-enhancing solutions – in our Tornado Cash Alternatives Briefing note . Railgun Railgun Elliptic’s research suggests that a significant portion of funds – estimated at around 70% – that has been sent through Railgun to date are funds from the Harmony hack. This suggests that since the OFAC sanctions on Tornado Cash, North Korea may be turning to lower obfuscating services as an alternative. However, the fact that funds from the Harmony hack comprised such a substantial volume of the Ether passing through Railgun renders the mixing ineffective. As an analogy, imagine if you threw five pennies into a jar full of 100 pennies, it would be extremely difficult for someone to determine which pennies were yours. However, if you threw 70 pennies into a jar with only 30 other pennies in it, then there would be a higher chance of linking those 70 specific pennies back to you. Mixers work in a similar way: when the anonymity set – or volume of other funds in the mixer is low – it makes the mixer less effective at concealing disproportionately large funds transfers. On-chain data shows that after sending the funds through Railgun, the Lazarus Group has since deposited funds into three cryptoasset exchanges. Two, namely Binance and Huobi, have announced that they have identified, blocked and seized a portion of the funds. This case demonstrates the importance of cryptoasset exchanges utlizing blockchain analytics solutions to identify transactions involving mixing services abused by sanctioned actors such as North Korea. Cryptocurrency Community Is Making It Difficult for North Korean Hackers To Profit September 8, 2022 | Erin Plante One of the most troubling trends in crypto crime right now is the stunning rise in funds stolen from DeFi protocols , and in particular cross-chain bridges . Much of the value stolen from DeFi protocols can be attributed to bad actors affiliated with North Korea, especially elite hacking units like Lazarus Group. We estimate that so far in 2022, North Korea-linked groups have stolen approximately $1 billion of cryptocurrency from DeFi protocols. But today I had the privilege of joining the Axie Infinity team on stage at AxieCon to deliver some good news: With the help of law enforcement and leading organizations in the cryptocurrency industry, more than $30 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers has been seized. This marks the first time ever that cryptocurrency stolen by a North Korean hacking group has been seized, and we’re confident it won’t be the last. These are the results thus far of our investigation following the March 2022 theft of more than $600 million from Ronin Network, a sidechain built for the play-to-earn game Axie Infinity. I am proud to say that the Chainalysis Crypto Incident Response team played a role in these seizures, utilizing advanced tracing techniques to follow stolen funds to cash out points and liaising with law enforcement and industry players to quickly freeze funds. The seizures represent approximately 10% of the total funds stolen from Axie Infinity (accounting for price differences between time stolen and seized), and demonstrate that it is becoming more difficult for bad actors to successfully cash out their ill-gotten crypto gains. We have proven that with the right blockchain analysis tools, world-class investigators and compliance professionals can collaborate to stop even the most sophisticated hackers and launderers. There is still work to be done, but this is a milestone in our efforts to make the cryptocurrency ecosystem safer. So, how did we do it? Here’s what we can share now. How the Ronin Bridge was hacked & the stolen funds were laundered The attack began when the Lazarus Group gained access to five of the nine private keys held by transaction validators for Ronin Network’s cross-chain bridge. They used this majority to approve two transactions, both withdrawals: one for 173,600 ether (ETH) and the other for 25.5 million USD Coin (USDC). They then initiated their laundering process – and Chainalysis began tracing the funds. The laundering of these funds has leveraged over 12,000 different crypto addresses to-date, which demonstrates the hackers’ highly sophisticated laundering capabilities. North Korea’s typical DeFi laundering technique has roughly five stages: Stolen Ether sent to intermediary wallets Ether mixed in batches using Tornado Cash Ether swapped for bitcoin Bitcoin mixed in batches Bitcoin deposited to crypto-to-fiat services for cashout Lazarus Group has replicated this process with large portions of Ronin’s stolen funds. We can visualize it below using Chainalysis Reactor: However, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) recently sanctioned Tornado Cash for its role in laundering over $455 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Axie Infinity. Since then, Lazarus Group has moved away from the popular Ethereum mixer, instead leveraging DeFi services to chain hop, or switch between several different kinds of cryptocurrencies in a single transaction. Bridges serve an important function to move digital assets between chains and most usage of these platforms is completely legitimate. Lazarus appears to be using bridges in an attempt to obscure source of funds. With Chainalysis tools these cross chain funds movements are easily traced. We can use Chainalysis Storyline to see an example of how Lazarus Group utilized chain-hopping to launder some of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity: Above, we see that the hacker bridged ETH from the Ethereum blockchain to the BNB chain and then swapped that ETH for USDD, which was then bridged to the BitTorrent chain. Lazarus Group carried out hundreds of similar transactions across several blockchains to launder the funds they stole from Axie Infinity, in addition to the more conventional Tornado Cash-based laundering we covered above. Transparency and collaboration are key Cryptocurrency’s transparency is instrumental to investigating hacks like the one suffered by Axie Infinity. Investigators with the right tools can follow the money to understand and disrupt a cybercrime organization’s laundering activities. This would never be possible in traditional financial channels, where money laundering usually involves networks of shell companies and financial institutions in jurisdictions that may not cooperate. Even so, these seizures would not have been possible without collaboration across the public and private sectors. Much of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity remain unspent in cryptocurrency wallets under the hackers’ control. We look forward to continuing to work with the cryptocurrency ecosystem to prevent them and other illicit actors from cashing out their funds. FAQs All your questions, answered Community Webinars Newsroom Partners Success story Global crypto exchange realizes $3.1M efficiency gain with Elliptic Global crypto exchange realizes $3.1M efficiency gain with Elliptic Uncover the story Company & Careers About Elliptic Security & Trust Careers Contact Sign in Get a demo Insights & research Mar 29, 2022 DeFi North Korea’s Lazarus Group identified as exploiters behind $540 million Ronin bridge heist North Korea’s Lazarus Group identified as exploiters behind $540 million Ronin bridge heist By Elliptic Intel [Update: this blog has been updated to reflect US sanctions announced against the Ronin Bridge Exploiter’s Ethereum address on April 14th 2022] On March 29th, the Ronin Network announced that 173,600 Ether (ETH) and 25.5 million USD Coins had been stolen from the Ronin cross-chain bridge six days earlier. The total value of the stolen cryptoassets at the time of the theft was $540 million. This is the second largest crypto theft of all time. On April 14th, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions against the thief's Ethereum address and listed the owner of this address as Lazarus Group – the North Korean state hacking group . The sanctions prohibit US persons and entities from transacting with this address to ensure the state-sponsored group can’t cash out any further funds they continue to hold onto through US-based crypto exchanges. The incident occurred six days before the exploit was announced by Ronin. Amid confusion over the delayed response, it announced that the exploit was only discovered after a 5,000 ETH withdrawal attempt from one of their users failed. At the time of discovery, the stolen funds were worth over $615 million. How the hack unfolded How the hack unfolded According to a postmortem published by Ronin, the theft came as a result of an attacker hacking the “validator nodes”of the Ronin bridge. Funds can be moved out if five of the nine validators approve it. The attacker managed to get hold of the private cryptographic keys belonging to five of the validators, which was enough to steal the cryptoassets. The post mortem claims that “all evidence points to this attack being socially engineered, rather than a technical flaw ”. Laundering the stolen crypto Laundering the stolen crypto Elliptic’s internal analysis indicates that the attacker has managed to launder 18% of their stolen funds as of April 14th. First, the stolen USDC was swapped for ETH through decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to prevent it from being seized. Tokens such as stablecoins are controlled by their issuers, who in some cases can freeze tokens involved in illicit activity. By converting the tokens at DEXs, the hacker avoided the anti-money laundering (AML) and 'know your customer' (KYC) checks performed at centralized exchanges. This is an increasingly common tactic seen in hacks of this type, as described in Elliptic’s recent report: “ DeFi: Risk, Regulation, and the Rise of DeCrime ” . However, the attacker then began laundering $16.7 million worth of ETH through three centralized exchanges. This strategy is uncommon for typical DeFi exploits given these exchanges’ AML obligations, though it has been observed more often in past Lazarus group-affiliated exploits. As the affected exchanges publicly announced that they would work with law enforcement to establish their identity, the attacker changed their laundering strategy to instead make use of Tornado Cash – a popular smart contract-based mixer on the Ethereum blockchain. Ongoing transactions have so far sent $80.3 million worth of ETH through Tornado Cash. Destination of $107 million ETH of the stolen $540 million ETH & USDC. The attacker’s blockchain activity shows that another $9.7 million worth of ETH is in intermediary wallets prepared to be laundered, most likely also through Tornado Cash. This leaves a considerable $433 million remaining in the attacker’s original wallet. Elliptic investigators are tracking these stolen funds, and have labelled the addresses associated to this attacker in our systems – ensuring that our clients will be alerted if they receive any of these funds. How the Lazarus Group is laundering its funds. Source: Elliptic Forensics . Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group refers to a group of North Korean state hackers who have been targeting crypto entities since at least 2017. Until 2021, the majority of this activity was directed towards centralized exchanges located in South Korea or elsewhere in Asia. However, within the past year the group’s attention has turned to DeFi services. While the service that was attacked in this instance – Ronin Network’s bridge – is decentralized, the creators of the network Sky Mavis are located in Vietnam. It is somewhat unsurprising that this attack has been attributed to North Korea. Many features of the attack mirrored the method used by Lazarus Group in previous high-profile attacks, including the location of the victim, the attack method (believed to have involved social engineering) and the laundering pattern utilized by the group after the event. Many commentators believe that cryptoassets stolen by Lazarus Group are used to fund the state’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs. With recent reports that North Korea may be again preparing for nuclear testing, today’s sanctions activity highlights the importance of ensuring that Lazarus Group is not able to successfully launder the proceeds of these attacks.
